Minimum technical points: compare per-GPU memory, communication topology, layer partitioning, batch and microbatch behavior, synchronization, latency target, and failure/reconfiguration costs.
corrected_answer:
Analytical stance under test: Stance 150 - Power and clock behaviour couples the two axes, because a tensor-parallel arm concentrates synchronous compute bursts that can trip power capping while a pipeline arm spreads them out.

Common frame (applies to every stance below).
Assumptions (must be restated by the answering engineer, not inherited silently):
A1. Single node, 8 GPUs, NVLink/NVSwitch intra-node; inter-node paths only appear where a stance says so explicitly.
A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: the SLO is TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, never a mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with at least 20% KV-cache headroom at target concurrency.
A4. Exactly one variable moves per arm: no simultaneous change of quantization, batching policy, or speculative decoding.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. Over PCIe-only or across nodes on RoCE/IB the same collective's latency floor rises roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce payload is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, which is small, so the collective is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and the per-hop latency floor dominates).
- B2. If the model cannot fit on one GPU, sharding is mandatory and the question reduces to which axis, not whether.
- B3. Under high, steady concurrency the PP bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: use TP inside the node up to the point where collective cost stops being repaid by reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross a node boundary or to fit a model TP alone cannot fit. PP is not a latency optimization.
Measurement and evidence policy: every number below that was not produced by a run on this hardware is labelled ESTIMATE and carries its derivation. Only values read out of named benchmark artifacts may be labelled MEASURED. This review reports no MEASURED values, because no benchmark was executed for it.

Tensor parallelism makes all ranks execute the same GEMM at the same instant, so the node's instantaneous power draw is highly correlated across GPUs; pipeline parallelism staggers stage execution and flattens the aggregate draw. When a node sits near its power or thermal envelope, the correlated burst can trigger clock capping, which appears in the measurement as a tensor-parallel scaling failure but is actually an enclosure-level constraint. Falsifiable hypothesis H150: locking SM and memory clocks to a sustainable floor will shrink the run-to-run variance of the tensor-parallel arm's TPOT p95 by more than it shrinks the pipeline arm's, and will reduce or remove any apparent super-linear tensor-parallel penalty (ESTIMATE; derivation: correlated draw across ranks raises peak enclosure power for the same average work, and any capping event stalls every rank simultaneously because the collective is a barrier). Controlled experiment: run each layout twice, once with default auto-boost and once with clocks pinned, and record per-GPU clock, power draw and throttle-reason counters at sub-second resolution alongside the latency series; the decision is only valid if the throttle-reason counters stay clean in the arm you intend to ship. Rollback gate: if pinned clocks are required to hold the SLO, the layout ships only with the clock policy encoded in the deployment manifest, and any node that reports a throttle reason during canary drains itself back to the previous layout.

Continuous-batching engines admit requests until KV-cache blocks run out, then preempt or recompute. Because tensor parallelism and pipeline parallelism leave different amounts of KV capacity per GPU, the two arms silently run at different admission depths, and the p95 tail is then produced by preemption events rather than by collective or bubble cost. Falsifiable hypothesis H151: fixing max concurrent sequences and max KV blocks to the smaller arm's capacity in both arms will move the two arms' TPOT p95 measurably closer together, and the residual gap is the true parallelism effect (ESTIMATE; derivation: preemption forces recompute of an entire prefix, whose cost is proportional to prompt length and therefore lands in the tail, not the median). Controlled experiment: three arms - tensor layout at native capacity, pipeline layout at native capacity, and both clamped to a common admission ceiling - with preemption and recompute counters exported per arm. Report the tail with and without the clamp. Rollback gate: ship only the clamped configuration whose preemption rate stays at or below the incumbent's during canary; a layout that wins on median but raises preemption rate is rejected.

Latency per request is dominated by the number of decode steps, and decode steps are set by generated token count. Rollback gate: a layout change is only accepted if it wins under fixed-length decode and does not regress output quality on the held-out prompt set under natural termination.

Tensor sharding requires the attention head count and the MLP intermediate dimension to divide by the tensor degree; when they do not, the stack either refuses the configuration or pads, and padding wastes both compute and memory bandwidth on every step. This is a structural constraint that must be checked before any experiment is designed, because an infeasible or padded arm is not a fair comparison point. Controlled experiment: enumerate the feasible tensor degrees from the model config before running anything, then benchmark only feasible degrees, capturing per-kernel efficiency counters to separate a padding effect from a collective effect. Rollback gate: any layout requiring padding is rejected by default; if it must ship, it ships behind a canary with an explicit efficiency-regression threshold and a one-command revert to the previously validated degree.
